How Ground Truth Shapes Retrieval Scores: Evidence-Aware Evaluation of a Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Breast Lesions

Miguel Mochizuki Silva Affiliation: Universidade Federal da Paraíba (UFPB), João Pessoa, PB, Brazil    Samuel Ismael Affiliation: Universidade Federal da Paraíba (UFPB), João Pessoa, PB, Brazil    Mateus C. Dias Affiliation: Universidade Federal da Paraíba (UFPB), João Pessoa, PB, Brazil    Thais Gaudêncio Affiliation: Universidade Federal da Paraíba (UFPB), João Pessoa, PB, Brazil    Yuri Malheiros Affiliation: Universidade Federal da Paraíba (UFPB), João Pessoa, PB, Brazil    Bruno Barufaldi Affiliation: Department of Radiology, Perelman School of Medicine,University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA, USA*Corresponding author: bruno.barufaldi@pennmedicine.upenn.edu
Abstract

Purpose: Retrieval scores for clinical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) are usually reported against annotated chunk per queries, which mixes retriever quality with annotation coverage. To describe the corpus, RAG (RAG) pipeline, and evidence-aware retrieval evaluation protocol developed for a question-answering system over the breast lesion management literature and to report retrieval performance under the selected configuration.

Methods: An 18-document corpus focused on breast lesions was used for retrieval benchmarking, ground-truth construction, and generation evaluation. One simple and direct evaluation query was created for each document, resulting in an 18-query development benchmark composed of Yes/No and WH-questions. Retrieval combines dense embeddings, BM25, and a cross-encoder reranker. Chunk size (128–1024 tokens), chunk overlap (0–20%) varied one factor at time, and four retriever configurations were compared in an ablation. Ground-truth relevance is defined at the level of evidence spans, which are mapped to every chunk containing them, so that chunks expressing the same underlying fact under overlapping chunking are scored as equivalent rather than as competing candidates. Retrieval quality is reported with R-Precision, Recall@K, MRR, and nDCG@K on an 18-query ground-truth development set. Generation quality was assessed in a separate experiment on an 512-token index, using DeepEval claim-level metrics with deepseek-v4-pro as the LLM judge, together with classical BLEU/ROUGE metrics across context depths K = 1–5.

Results: The selected hybrid retriever (384-token chunks, 20% overlap) retrieved accepted evidence in the top three results for 17 of 18 queries. Recall@3, R-Precision, MRR@3, and nDCG@3 each reached 0.94. Ground-truth curation increased the number of evidence spans from 25 to 37 and accepted chunk targets from 36 to 51 without changing retrieval rankings.

Conclusion: Cross-encoder reranking produced the highest retrieval scores. Ground-truth curation expanded the set of recognized evidence without changing retrieval rankings, underscoring the dependence of evaluation scores on relevance annotations. The small development set and retrieval-informed curation warrant independent validation, including radiologist assessment of evidence sufficiency.

1 Introduction

Management of benign and high-risk breast lesions requires integrating imaging findings, biopsy pathology, radiologic–pathologic concordance, and patient risk. Supporting evidence is distributed across society guidelines, appropriateness criteria, and lesion-specific studies, which may differ in their recommendations. For lesions of uncertain malignant potential (B3 lesions), international consensus supports vacuum-assisted excision as an alternative to open surgery for selected categories [rageth2019b3], whereas U.S. guidance permits imaging surveillance for selected radiologic–pathologic concordant lesions [asbrs2024highrisk]. Retrieving the correct recommendation therefore requires preserving the clinical conditions under which it applies.

Large language models (LLMs) encode substantial clinical knowledge [singhal2023medpalm] but may generate unsupported statements [ji2023hallucination]. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) conditions answers on retrieved passages and makes supporting sources available for inspection [lewis2020rag]. In medical question answering, retrieval has improved performance in some settings, although outcomes depend on the corpus and retrieval strategy [xiong2024medrag]. Missing evidence can limit answer correctness, while supplying additional passages does not necessarily resolve the problem because language models may fail to use relevant information in long contexts [liu2024lost].

Medical RAG systems have been evaluated using guidelines and clinical resources, including clinical question answering and simulated oncology cases [zakka2023almanac, ferber2025oncologyagent]. Radiology-focused studies have also reported improvements that vary across models and sources [tayebiarasteh2025radiorag, weinert2025radiographics]. However, evaluation protocols remain heterogeneous [amugongo2025ragreview], and expert assessment has identified retrieval and evidence selection as important failure points [kim2025rethinkingrag]. These findings motivate evaluating retrieved evidence separately from generated answers.

Retrieval scores depend on which passages are annotated as relevant. When a benchmark recognizes only one chunk per question, another chunk containing the same supporting evidence may be scored as nonrelevant. Overlapping segmentation makes such alternatives more likely, while additional relevant passages may remain unannotated. In information retrieval, incomplete relevance judgments have long been recognized as a source of evaluation bias [zobel1998reliable, buettcher2007biased, buckley2004incomplete]. The effects on individual metrics depend on their definitions and the accepted evidence targets; overlap alone does not establish a fixed penalty.

Question-answering benchmarks have represented supporting evidence through answer spans, sentence-level facts, and source provenance [rajpurkar2016squad, kwiatkowski2019naturalquestions, yang2018hotpotqa, petroni2021kilt]. In RAG evaluation, conventional ranking metrics may not fully capture whether retrieved passages supply the information needed to answer a question [yu2024ragsurvey]. Chunk-based evaluation is also sensitive to how evidence is partitioned and repeated across overlapping segments [smith2024chunking]. Evidence-level relevance annotations can therefore reduce dependence on a single chunk identifier, provided that accepted alternatives are explicitly defined and audited.

We present RAG-MAMA, a retrieval-augmented generation system evaluated on a curated 18-document breast-lesion corpus and an 18-query development benchmark. We investigate whether incomplete ground-truth annotations can underestimate retrieval performance. Canonical evidence spans are defined independently of chunk identifiers and mapped to each segmentation configuration. We distinguish alternative supporting chunks from complementary evidence requirements, audit previously unrecognized evidence while keeping retrieval rankings fixed, and separately evaluate retrieval configurations and generation quality. The system focuses on excision-versus-surveillance decisions, with fixed deferral for excluded categories. This study establishes a small-scale methodological baseline rather than demonstrating clinical effectiveness or validity on more complex, multi-evidence questions.

2 Methods

Figure 1 shows the RAG-MAMA pipeline. The corpus comprised 18 papers, which were preprocessed and split into 757 chunks (size 384, overlap 77). Each query was retrieved in parallel by a dense retriever (BGE-Large) and a lexical retriever (BM25). The two ranked lists were combined with Reciprocal Rank Fusion and reranked with a BGE cross-encoder. The top-K chunks were passed to Qwen 3.6 (27B) to generate a grounded answer. Retrieval was evaluated with ranking metrics and generation with DeepEval.

2.1 Corpus Compilation, Pre-processing, and Quality Assurance

The corpus was scoped a priori to a fixed reference table of 15 breast pathology categories defined by the American Society of Breast Surgeons (ASBrS) high-risk lesion taxonomy [asbrs2024highrisk].

Thirty candidate documents were assembled by purposive expert selection, comprising society guidelines, American College of Radiology (ACR) appropriateness criteria, World Health Organization (WHO) classification, and lesion-specific primary literature. Documents were eligible if they provided management recommendations, upgrade-risk estimates, radiologic–pathologic concordance criteria, or nomenclature definitions for at least one retrieval-eligible category. Each was evaluated by category-specific term frequency and adjudicated by full-text review. Malignant categories and fibromatosis/desmoid tumor are not answered by retrieval: a scope gate applied to the normalized pathology label returns a fixed deferral before retrieval runs. Fibromatosis is excluded because current sarcoma guidance favors active surveillance over the excision and desmoid text remains in the indexed corpus.

Classification and typical management of benign, high-risk, and malignant breast pathology entities. Malignant lesions are routed to a fixed response by the scope gate.
